messages.content:
Validate the following vignette.

Patient demographics:
  age: 74
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Software Engineer
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 75

Patient-reported symptoms:
  Triggers: Auditory (Silence): Sudden or complete silence, Olfactory (Hospital): Hospital or antiseptic smell, Auditory (Cars): Car sounds
  Threat: Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Shame on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense shame, Emotion Without Image: Sometimes I feel the full emotional intensity of the event without any clear image or memory
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me, Self-Blame: The event happened because of the way I acted

Vignette:
Lien, a 74-year-old software engineer with a career spanning from punch cards to the cloud, presented as a woman held captive by a memory fifteen years old. The event itself was a blur of speed and silence, a single afternoon that had unraveled the quiet order of her life. Her son, Bao, then sixteen, had suffered a severe anaphylactic reaction to a new medication. Lien had been working in her home office, so absorbed in a complex line of code that the house’s stillness didn't register until it was too late. It was the silence she remembered first—a profound, unnatural quiet that had pulled her from her screen. She found Bao in the living room, blue-lipped and unconscious. For a frozen moment, she could only stare, a chasm of helplessness opening beneath her. She had come to believe that this hesitation, these lost seconds, were the hinge upon which the entire catastrophe turned. The memory of her husband’s frantic driving to the hospital was not a visual one, but a roar in her ears—the desperate, straining sound of the engine that she now hears in every passing car.

In the years since Bao’s full recovery, the world has become a treacherous landscape for Lien. She operates under the constant, exhausting assumption that the world is a fundamentally dangerous place, a belief reinforced by her own perceived failure to protect her son. This vigilance is most acute at night. Sleep offers no refuge; instead, she lies awake for hours, straining to hear over the sound of her own heartbeat, certain that she must remain alert to avert some unseen, impending disaster. Any sudden quiet, the very state she once required for the deep concentration her work demands, now triggers a jolt of pure panic. A lull in conversation at dinner, the moment after the air conditioner clicks off—these silences are not empty, but filled with a terrible premonition. She has learned to manage this at work by keeping a constant low-level stream of podcasts or classical music playing in her headphones, a buffer of noise that keeps the threatening stillness at bay.

The past is not a static memory for Lien but an active, recurring assault. When she intentionally recalls the hospital—the sharp, antiseptic smell that now clings to hand sanitizers and cleaning products, making her recoil—the terror is as fresh and paralyzing as it was that day. With it comes a wave of shame so intense it feels like a physical blow, a confirmation of her own inadequacy. More unsettling are the moments when the feeling arrives without a story. She might be walking through the grocery store when an overwhelming sense of dread and helplessness washes over her, a full-body emotional echo of the event, but with no clear image or thought attached. It leaves her disoriented and breathless, fighting a ghost she cannot see.

Over time, these experiences have calcified into a rigid set of behaviors. She avoids driving with her husband, the sound of a rapidly accelerating car being too much to bear. She video calls Bao, now a father himself, multiple times a day, a constant checking that he knows is rooted in love but which has become a source of gentle friction. The final impetus for seeking therapy came last month, when her grandson developed a mild fever. Lien’s reaction was one of catastrophic panic, an insistence on an emergency room visit that frightened her daughter-in-law and deeply worried her husband. It was then she realized she could no longer distinguish between a potential threat and a certain one, and that her inability to stop bad things from happening had transformed into an expectation that they always would. She has come to therapy not for a cure, but with the fragile hope of learning to live in the quiet moments again without being certain that danger is about to strike.
